kicker: Message threads on the Claude API

scenes.headline: How a message thread keeps your conversation server-side
scenes.sub: Send the history once, then only what is new.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Purl! Here is how message threads stop an agent re-uploading its whole conversation every turn.

scenes.text: The API holds the conversation in memory between turns, so each request carries only the new messages and the previous response id.
scenes.say: The API keeps the conversation in memory between turns. So each request carries only the new messages, and the id of the previous response.

left.title: Stateless request
left.say: Without a thread, every step uploads the system prompt, the tools and every earlier message again.

right.title: Continue request
right.say: With a thread, it sends the newest tool result and one id. The model still reads everything.

steps.say: The first request is ordinary. Full conversation, system prompt and tools, plus a thread field that says create.
The API stores the conversation and the reply under the response id, in memory, never on disk.
Each continue sends only the new messages. The API rebuilds the conversation and the model reads all of it.
After five idle minutes the thread is gone. The client gets not found, and replays everything from its own copy.

scenes.title: Uploaded over a 120-request coding loop
scenes.say: I drove the real software kit against a mock server. Fifty-one point seven seven megabytes without a thread, zero point seven eight with one.

scenes.title: Two clocks, both five minutes
scenes.say: A thread and the prompt cache are separate, but they run out together.

items.say: Say the agent pauses for six minutes.
The thread has expired, so the next request uploads the whole conversation again.
The default cache has expired too, so the whole prefix is billed as a cache write.
A one-hour cache keeps the tokens cheap across the pause, but every write costs more.

scenes.text: A thread saves upload and latency; prompt caching still decides what every token costs.
scenes.say: A thread saves upload and time to first token. Prompt caching still decides what every token costs.
Create once, continue with deltas, keep your own copy, and let caching set the bill.
